doc.title: Steve Turré interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, November 29, 2021

title: Arranging for conch shells and the 12-bar blues
summary: Rowe asks about arranging for shells; Turré explains each has about a fourth of range and says the blues is the root young players neglect.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: What the blues is, and why every jazz player needs it

blocks.x: That’s terrific. That’s a wonderful story. And I watched a concert you did, I believe it was in Vienna. And you had — not only were you playing a shell but your had your brass section. And from an arranging standpoint it must be a different kind of challenge to have this group of shells and find four or five that have a range that are not only playable but that can be manipulated into whatever your compositional ideas area. Is that a fair statement? Because there was one thing you did that was like a 12-bar blues. And the conch shells are going [scats] these great licks. But how do you deal with the various pitches that they make because of the physics of the thing?

Well every shell has a range. And most of them have about a fourth. You have your primary tone, and then you put your hand in it and it lowers the pitch. Kind of like a French horn you know. And so if you have a fourth to work with [scats] that’s six half- steps. So you’ve got a smaller shell is higher pitch and a bigger shell is lower pitch. You’ve got a lot of notes you can work with. And if you move a half step in any direction you’re going to be in the court. So you just figure it out you know, you work with what you have.
There was one time during that piece where you were playing a smaller shell and a unison melody with one of your players, it had a very large shell. I don’t have the word © Fillius Jazz Archive -10-
for it, that 12-bar blues is such a versatile musical form and to hear it played with four shells was just outstanding.

It’s the roots of jazz. You know the way I came up, and unfortunately a lot of the young players not only can’t play the blues they don’t want to play the blues. That really bothers me, because that’s the root of the music. The more you have an understanding of the blues the more you can express whatever you do. Because the blues come from here, not from here. It’s not mathematic.
